title: Comprehensive Acute GIT Bleeding & Haemostasis Management
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide covering the classification, emergency management, and prognostic scoring of Upper and Lower GI bleeding, alongside an in-depth approach to coagulation disorders, anticoagulant therapies, and surgical considerations.

Lower GI bleeding (below the ligament of Treitz)

sections.title: Upper GIT Bleeding: Causes
content: Esophagus: Esophagitis, Esophageal varices, Esophageal cancer
Stomach: Gastric ulcer (40%), Gastritis, Gastric cancer
Duodenum: Duodenal ulcer, Aortoenteric fistula (if previous aortic graft)
Mallory Weiss tear: mucosal tear at gastro-esophageal junction due to retching
Coagulopathy
Drugs: alcohol, aspirin, NSAIDS, thrombolytics & anticoagulants
Renal disease
Liver disease

rows: Vomiting of blood: frequency, volume of blood
Black tarry stool: usually due to upper GI bleeding. Occurs when blood comes in contact with hydrochloric acid in the gut. Only need > 50 ml of blood loss.
Bright red or maroon rectal bleeding: Usually a sign of a lower GI bleed & rarely seen unless the patient is having a very large, brisk upper GI bleed ( > 1000 ml).
Postural dizziness, fainting, abdominal pain, dysphagia, Chest pain, dyspnea & syncope.
Cool & clammy skin. Vital signs: Pulse (tachycardia), Bl.P (hypotension & postural changes). Urine output & JVP: decreased. Jaundice: biliary colic + jaundice + melaena suggests haemobilia.

sections.title: Emergency Shock Assessment
content: Cool and clammy skin
Pulse > 100 bpm
Systolic BP < 100mm Hg
JVP < 1cm H2O
Urine output < 30mL/h

sections.title: Management Strategy: Shocked vs. Not Shocked
content: If Not Shocked: Insert 2 big cannulae (14-16G), start slow saline IVI (to keep lines patent), check bloods & monitor vital signs + urine output.
If Shocked Step 1: Protect airway (endotracheal intubation to prevent aspiration in massive bleeding or mental status change) and give high flow oxygen.
If Shocked Step 2: Insert 2 big cannulae. Draw bloods for laboratory investigations & Cross match 6 units.
If Shocked Step 3: Rapid IV crystalloid infusion (normal saline or ringer lactate) up to 1L.
If Shocked Step 4: If still shocked, give group specific blood or group O Rh –ve until cross matching is done (transfuse as dictated by haemodynamics).
NB: Avoid saline in patients with decompensated liver disease (ascites, peripheral oedema).

sections.title: Ongoing Management & Monitoring
content: Correct clotting abnormalities (Vit k, FFP, platelet concentrates)
Set up CVP line to guide fluid replacement
Catheterize and monitor urine output (aim for > 30 mL/h)
Vital signs monitoring every 15min until stable, then every 1h
Notify surgeons of all severe bleeds
Keep NPO
Nasogastric tube placement (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube): if massive or continuous bleeding for aspiration & lavage
ECG: looking for signs of ischemia or infarct (inferior MI)
Proton pump inhibitors: e.g omeprazole 40 mg PO to prevent stress ulcers
Eradicate Helicobacter pylori if +ve

sections.title: The Role of Endoscopy
sections.content: Endoscopy can identify the source of bleeding, estimate the risk of rebleeding +/- therapeutic intervention (e.g varices ligation/injection therapy, injection therapy for ulcer, heat probe thermocoagulation, hemoclip or laser). It should be performed early after volume resuscitation. Risks for rebleeding include spurting or oozing, visible vessel or fibrin clot. NB: If site not identified; bleeding site healed; nose bleed (swallowed blood); site distal to 3rd part of duodenum. NB: UGI barium studies are contraindicated in acute bleed as they interfere with endoscopy/surgery.

content.explanation: Age > 60; Signs of shock (pulse > 100 bpm, SBP < 100 mmhg); Significant co-morbidity (renal/liver failure or malignancy); Bleeding diathesis.

branches: Small Bowel: Neoplasm, Meckel’s diverticulum, Crohn’s, Aortoenteric fistula, Vascular problems
Colon: Diverticuli, Angiodysplasia, IBD (UC/Crohn's), Ischemic gut, Neoplasm, Infectious
Coagulopathy: Drugs, renal disease, liver disease

rows: Site distal to the pylorus; Must rule out massive UGIB!
Likely diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, or aortoenteric fistula
Recent ingestion of poorly cooked meat

sections.title: Lower GI Management & Diagnostics
content: ABC Management: Priority volume resuscitation.
Stable Patients: Clinical follow-up with volume/blood as needed; prep for colonoscopy once settled.
Tagged RBC Scan (TRBC): 99mTc labels RBCs (last 48h); accurate to 80%; detects rates as low as 0.1 ml/min. Screening for arteriography.
Angiography: Rapid localization/therapy when rates > 0.5 ml/min; identifies site in 60%; therapeutic vasopressin or embolization.
Colonoscopy: Not useful in ongoing bleeding; best for stabilized patients with bowel purge. Barium enemas contraindicated in acute setting.
Surgery: For ongoing bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or failure of other therapeutic maneuvers.

sections.title: 3 Sets of Questions for Bleeding Disorders

content.explanation: 1. Is there an emergency (exsanguination, hypovolaemia, CNS bleeding)? 2. Why is the patient bleeding (Normal context, secondary cause like drugs/alcohol, pattern indicative of vascular/platelet/coagulation, family history)? 3. What is the mechanism (Clotting screen results)?

sections.title: Coagulation Test Definitions
sections.content: 1. Prothrombin Time (PT) & INR: Measures extrinsic and common pathways (Factors I, II, V, VII, X). PT normal: 11-16s. INR standardizes results (Normal: 0.9–1.3; Warfarin target: 2.0–3.0). Prolonged by Vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, liver disease, or DIC. 2. aPTT: Measures intrinsic and common pathways (Factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII). Normal: 35-45s. Prolonged by Heparin, haemophilia, DIC, liver disease. 3. Thrombin Time (TT): Measures fibrinogen to fibrin conversion. Normal: 10-15s. Prolonged by Heparin, DIC, dysfibrinogenaemia. 4. D-dimers: Fibrin degradation product. Increased in DIC, DVT, PE, infection, or malignancy. 5. Bleeding Time: Assesses platelet function (Platelet count N: 150k-400k). Normal <7 mins. Prolonged in thrombocytopenia, DIC, or antiplatelet use. Seldom performed now.

sections.title: Management of Bleeding Disorders
sections.content: Resuscitate if shocked. Discuss need for FFP/Platelets with a haematologist for massive transfusion or clotting disorders. ITP: Steroids +/- IV immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: Consult expert. Haemophilia: Factor replacement; Never give IM injections. Drugs Categories: 1. Coagulants (Vit. K, Ethamsylate). 2. Anticoagulants (Heparin/Warfarin). 3. Antiplatelets (Aspirin/Clopidogrel). 4. Fibrinolytics (Streptokinase/tPA). 5. Antifibrinolytics (Tranexamic acid).

rows: Binds Antithrombin III; inhibits IIa, Xa, IXa

sections.title: Heparin Details & Warnings
content: S/E: Bleeding, Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), Osteoporosis
HIT/Osteoporosis less common with LMWH; Beware hyperkalaemia
Contraindications: Bleeding disorders, previous HIT, peptic ulcer, cerebral haemorrhage, severe hypertension, neurosurgery

rows: Inhibits Vit K regeneration; analogous to deficiency
Peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, hypertension, pregnancy
Vit K 5-10mg IV; PCC (50u/kg) or FFP

sections.title: Initiating Therapeutic Anticoagulation
content: Step 1: Use LMWH or UFH initially; give Warfarin in combination from Day 1.
Step 2: Continue Heparin until INR reached and until Day 5 (Warfarin has initial prothrombotic effect).
Step 3 (UFH Bolus): 5000iu IV over 30min (10,000iu if severe PE).
Step 4 (UFH Infusion): 25,000iu in 50mL saline; start 1000-2000iu/h. Aim for aPTT ratio 1-2.
Step 5 (Warfarin Start): 10mg PO Day 1; Lower dose (5-10mg) if >60yrs, liver disease, or cardiac failure.

sections.title: Surgery & Antiplatelets
content: Minor Surgery: May proceed if INR within 24h is < 3.5.
Major Surgery: Stop drugs 2-5 days pre-op; Individual risk/benefit assessment.
Emergency Surgery: Vitamin K (10mg IV) +/- FFP may be required.
Elective Conversion: Conversion to heparin (stop 6h prior to surgery); Monitor aPTT.
Antiplatelet Mechanism: Aspirin irreversibly inactivates cyclo-oxygenase (Thromboxane A2/Prostacyclin inhibition).
Aspirin Reversal: Effects reversed by 5 days after stopping.
Clopidogrel: Less gastric irritation; used for aspirin intolerance or post-coronary stent.

sections.title: Hyperviscosity Syndrome
content: Definition: Viscosity rise impairs microcirculation due to high RBC, WBC, or plasma components (immunoglobulins).
Causes: Polycythaemia rubra vera, Leukaemia, Multiple myeloma (IgG 55%, IgA 25%), Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia (IgM).
Presentation: Lethargy & confusion, Spontaneous bleeding (GU/GI), Retinopathy (venous dilatation, segmentation, tortuosity, haemorrhages, exudates).
Treatment: Venesection (Polycythaemia), Leucopheresis (Leukaemias), Plasmapheresis (Myeloma/Waldenstrom's).
